title: Services through a personal service company
summary: A limited company supplies one individual's services. Includes the off-payroll working (IR35) responsibilities.

decision.hint: A limited company owned by the individual supplies their services; the Company records who decides off-payroll status, and the work is genuinely done as a business.

questions.label: Company
questions.help: The legal name of the Company, exactly as registered.

questions.label: Company email for notices
questions.help: The address the Supplier sends formal notices to.

questions.label: Supplier (registered company name)
questions.help: Exactly as shown at Companies House.

questions.label: Supplier signatory
questions.help: A director or other person authorised to sign for the Supplier.

questions.label: Operative (the individual who does the work)
questions.help: The person whose services the Supplier provides. Usually the Supplier's director and shareholder.

questions.label: Operative's role
questions.help: For example: door supervisor, security officer, CCTV operator, security consultant.

questions.label: Operative's link to the Supplier
questions.help: The off-payroll working rules (ITEPA 2003 Chapter 10) apply where the Operative holds a material interest (more than 5%) in the Supplier.

options.label: The Operative owns or controls more than 5% of the Supplier (a personal service company)
The Operative is an employee of the Supplier with no material interest
The Supplier is an umbrella company that employs the Operative

questions.label: Is the Company an SIA approved contractor?
questions.help: Approved contractors must deploy only employees or people treated as employees for tax (ACS indicator 4.2.1).

questions.label: The Services
questions.help: What the Supplier will do. Be specific; this defines the scope.

questions.label: Deliverables and standards
questions.help: The results and standards the Services must meet, for example reports, response times or service levels.

questions.label: Where the Services are provided
questions.help: Sites, areas or "remotely".

questions.label: How work is agreed
questions.help: Pick what really happens. If there is a regular rota the Supplier is expected to cover, do not pick "offered one at a time".

options.label: Assignments offered one at a time, free to accept or decline

questions.label: How Assignments are confirmed
questions.help: For example: "by email" or "through the Company's scheduling app".

questions.label: Commitments beyond agreed work
questions.help: Record what actually exists, for example "none" or "the Company will offer first refusal on work at site X". Do not overstate or understate it.

questions.label: Cancellation terms
questions.help: What happens if either party cancels agreed work, including any cancellation fee and how much notice is needed.

questions.label: Day-to-day contact at the Company
questions.help: Name or role.

options.label: Fixed fee for the Services
options.text: as a fixed fee for the Services

options.label: Per day
options.text: for each day of Services provided

options.label: Per hour
options.text: for each hour of Services provided

questions.label: Fee
questions.help: Excluding VAT.

questions.label: Payment terms
questions.help: For example "30 days". Statutory late-payment interest applies if the Company pays late.

questions.label: Status assessed by
questions.help: Name and role of the person at the Company who carried out the status assessment.

questions.label: Company's size under the off-payroll rules
questions.help: Medium or large if, for its last financial year, the Company (or its group) met two or more of HMRC's size tests for turnover, balance sheet and employees. Check the current thresholds on GOV.UK. A small client does not decide status.

options.label: Medium or large: the Company decides status
Small: the Supplier decides under Chapter 8
Made: the off-payroll rules do not apply

questions.label: Date the status determination statement was given
Person responsible for status decisions
questions.help: The person at the Company who makes and records status determinations and reassessments.

questions.label: Where disagreements are sent
questions.help: Name, role and email address.

questions.label: Equipment the Supplier provides
questions.help: What the Supplier really provides at its own cost.

questions.label: Equipment the Company or client provides
questions.help: For example keys, radios, body-worn cameras. Write "nothing" if none.

questions.label: Professional indemnity insurance required?
questions.help: Usually needed for advice, design, consultancy or reports the Company relies on.

questions.label: Other insurance required
questions.help: Optional, for example motor insurance for business use.

questions.label: Do the Services include SIA-licensable conduct?
Notice to end the agreement
questions.help: For example "one week". Applies to both parties.

questions.label: Limit on the Supplier's liability
questions.help: An amount or a formula, for example the fees paid in the previous contract year. Take advice on what is reasonable.

assessment.title: Status assessment
assessment.intro: Answer from what really happens on site, not from what the agreement says. Employment rights and tax are decided separately. Working through a company does not by itself make the Operative independent. For tax, "self employed" here means the off-payroll working rules do not apply; "off payroll" means they do.

questions.label: In practice, who does the work?
questions.help: Describe what really happens, not what a contract says. Clothing, a phone, a torch or travel to work do not make the Operative a business.

options.label: A business that decides who does the work and has its own staff or associates

questions.label: If the Operative cannot attend, can the Supplier genuinely send someone else?
questions.help: A substitution right only counts if the Supplier really chooses, engages and pays the replacement, and the Company has no veto beyond checking the replacement is licensed, screened and competent. If the Company always finds the cover, or approves people at its discretion, the answer is not "real".

options.label: Yes: the Supplier chooses, engages and pays the replacement; the Company only checks licence, screening and competence
Only someone the Company approves at its discretion
No: the Company finds the cover, or the work is simply not done

questions.label: Who has the right to decide how, when and where the work is done?
questions.help: Count the right to control even if it is rarely used. Supervision, direction or control includes rotas, patrol routes, reporting routines and mandatory site procedures, even where those procedures come from regulation (HMRC ESM2037).

options.label: The Company or the client: they set times, tasks, routes or procedures and can tell the person how to work
The Operative: only the result and the legal or site requirements are set

questions.label: Does the Supplier carry real financial risk?
questions.help: For example: putting poor work right at its own cost, fixed prices that can make a loss, significant investment, or its own staff to pay. Paying for a uniform, phone, torch or travel to work is not financial risk.

options.label: No: paid for time, with no real risk of loss

questions.label: Who provides the equipment needed for the work?

options.label: The Supplier provides its own significant equipment
Shared: the Supplier provides some significant items, the Company or client the rest
The Company or the client provides it (beyond basic clothing and a phone)

questions.label: Does the Operative actually work for other customers?
questions.help: Actual work for others in business, not just being free to.

questions.label: What happens in practice about offering and accepting work?
questions.help: Look at the pattern, not the wording. A regular rota that is expected to be filled is an ongoing obligation even if each shift is "offered".

options.label: Each piece of work is genuinely offered and can be turned down without consequence
There is a regular pattern, or work is expected to be offered and accepted

questions.label: Is the Operative part of the Company's organisation?
questions.help: For example: wears the Company uniform as if staff, is on the Company rota, manages staff, or is treated like an employee.

questions.label: Where is the work done?
questions.help: If an end client directs the work, that client may be the "client" under the off-payroll working rules.

options.label: Works as part of the Company's own service, under the Company's contract with its client
Placed with an end client who directs the work day to day

assessment.mismatch: If the Operative is a worker or employee for employment rights, engage them directly on the worker, casual or permanent pack, or through a labour provider. Do not use a personal service company to avoid employment rights.

slots.why: Included because the assessment records that the Supplier carries real financial risk
Included because the Company decides status as a medium or large client
Included because professional indemnity cover is required
Included because other insurance is listed
Included because the Services are SIA-licensable
Included because the Services are SIA-licensable

rules.message: The wording gives the Supplier a right to send a substitute, but the status assessment does not record a real, workable substitution arrangement. Do not add a substitution right to make the engagement look independent. Use the wording that matches what happens (personal service, or replacements only with approval), or correct the assessment if a real right exists in practice.

any.wording: independent business|on (its|his|her|their) own account|in business on (its|his|her|their) own

rules.message: The wording describes the Supplier as an independent business, but the assessment does not show it: the Operative must decide how the work is done, carry real financial risk, actually work for other customers and not be part of the Company. Use the neutral status clause instead, or correct the assessment if it is wrong.

The wording says the Operative decides how the work is done, but the assessment records that the Company or the client has that control. Use the "Company requirements" delivery wording, which reflects the real arrangement.

The wording says each Assignment can be declined with no promise of work, but the assessment records a regular pattern or an expectation to offer and accept work. Record the real programme and commitments, or use the worker or employee route if that is what the arrangement is.
Part of the status assessment is "not clear yet", so this route needs review. Find out what actually happens on site before relying on this agreement, and take advice if it stays unclear.
The status outcome is recorded as unresolved, so this route requires review. Do not send the agreement until the employment and tax status have been decided, with advice if needed.

Confirm whether the Company is small or medium/large under the off-payroll rules before sending. It decides who determines status: the Company (medium or large) or the Supplier (small). Check the size tests on GOV.UK against the Company's last accounts, including its group.

Make the status determination with reasonable care and give the status determination statement, with reasons, to the Operative and the Supplier before the work starts. Until it is given, the Company is liable for the tax and National Insurance.

The determination says the off-payroll rules do not apply, but the assessment shows personal service under the Company's control. Review the determination: it must be made with reasonable care, or the Company stays liable for the tax.
The determination says the off-payroll rules apply, but the recorded tax outcome is "outside". Make the two consistent before sending.

As a small client, the Company does not decide status: the Supplier applies the Chapter 8 intermediaries rules. Keep evidence of the Company's size, confirm it if asked, and check it again before each tax year.

Inside the rules the Company is the fee-payer: set up PAYE on the deemed direct payment before the first invoice is paid. This is tax treatment only; it does not on its own give the Operative employment rights.

An umbrella company is not a personal service company. Use the labour provider pack, check that the umbrella operates PAYE on the Operative's pay, and remember the Company can be jointly liable for an umbrella's unpaid PAYE.

The Operative has no material interest in the Supplier, so the off-payroll rules do not apply. Check whether the agency rules apply instead (the Supplier, as an employment business, must operate PAYE) or whether the labour provider pack fits better.

The Operative is placed with an end client who directs the work. That client may be the "client" under the off-payroll rules who must decide status, and the Company would then be the fee-payer. Take advice on who determines status before sending.

The Operative works under the Company's control, as part of its organisation, with ongoing commitments. Working through a company does not make them independent: they may be a worker or employee for employment rights, and tax may still be due under PAYE. Check the employment outcome.

The Company is an SIA approved contractor. The ACS requires everyone it deploys to be an employee or an employee for tax purposes, and the current workbook does not allow personal service companies anywhere in an approved contractor's supply chain. Engage the Operative directly on payroll, or use a compliant labour provider, instead.

Paying by the hour or day with no real financial risk is a sign of employment or worker status. Check that the status outcome reflects this, and that the National Minimum Wage would be met if the person is a worker.

The assessment records that the Company or client provides the equipment. Make sure the equipment answers list those items, so the agreement matches what happens, and check this against the status outcome.
Read the SIA and HMRC guidance 'Learn how HMRC rules apply to the security operatives you deploy' and keep a record of how this engagement meets it.
In Northern Ireland, employment and worker rights come from the Employment Rights (Northern Ireland) Order 1996, and the Labour Relations Agency gives guidance. Tax status rules are UK-wide.
